The five trails

Cheshire Rail Trail

  • 45.3 mi
  • Bellows Falls to Winchendon

Rebuilt from Westmoreland through Keene to Troy. The Walpole end is not yet planned, and stretches near Fitzwilliam are in progress.

Parking: see the Parking layer on the interactive map.

Ashuelot Rail Trail

  • 21.2 mi
  • Keene to Hinsdale

Rebuilt near Keene and Swanzey. Winchester and Hinsdale stretches are in progress or unplanned.

Peterborough to Hillsborough

  • 20.1 mi
  • Peterborough to Hillsborough

A rebuilt middle section, with the ends not yet planned.

Monadnock Rail Trail

  • 15.4 mi
  • Peterborough to Winchendon

Short rebuilt stretches near Jaffrey, with the rest in progress or not yet planned. A 4 mi connector links to Winchendon, MA.

Fort Hill Rail Trail

  • 8.1 mi
  • Hinsdale to Brattleboro, VT

Work in progress. A bridge crosses the Connecticut River into Brattleboro.

About and donate

A volunteer-led nonprofit rebuilding the region's rail trails.

What we do

The Monadnock Region Rail Trail Collaborative brings together towns, nonprofits, snowmobile clubs and volunteers. We rehabilitate and maintain the Cheshire, Ashuelot, Fort Hill, Hillsborough and Monadnock rail trails.

The goal is a connected network linking southwest New Hampshire to Bellows Falls and Brattleboro, VT, and Winchendon, MA.

Who's on the board

  • Cheshire County
  • Keene
  • Keene Sno-riders
  • Jaffrey
  • Monadnock Conservancy
  • Southwest Region Planning Commission
  • Swanzey
  • Walpole
  • Winchester

How projects get funded

Federal Grants, State Grants, Towns, Private Funding, In-kind volunteer hours and equipment.

Westmoreland to Keene

  • About 12 mi one way
  • 24 mi round trip
  • Rebuilt the whole way
WestmorelandKeene
  • Good to know
    The whole route is rebuilt trail. Start from either end. Parking is on the interactive map.
  • Heads up
    Downed trees were reported near Westmoreland after storms. Check conditions before you go.
  • Not yet planned
    The trail north from Westmoreland toward Walpole has no work scheduled yet.

Keene to Troy, and beyond

  • About 12 mi one way
  • 24 mi round trip
  • First 2 mi still in progress
KeeneTroyFitzwilliam
  • Good to know
    Troy's restored depot is a natural stop, about 7 mi from Keene. Past Troy, rebuilt trail continues about 6 more miles.
  • Heads up
    A short stretch just southeast of Keene is still being finished. Expect rough ground or a detour.
  • Coming soon
    Work is under way on the last 3 or so miles into Fitzwilliam. This trip will get longer.

Westmoreland to Troy: the big day

  • About 19 mi one way
  • 38 mi round trip
  • About 2 mi in progress
WestmorelandKeeneTroy
  • Good to know
    Go one way and arrange a pickup, or turn around at Keene for a 24 mi round trip. Keene makes a good halfway stop.
  • Heads up
    Covers the in-progress stretch southeast of Keene, plus the downed trees reported near Westmoreland.
  • Coming soon
    The route will extend toward Fitzwilliam once work under way south of Troy is finished.

Shorter trips

Keene to Swanzey on the Ashuelot is about 5 miles of rebuilt trail. Around Peterborough, about 6 miles are rebuilt.

Railroad history

The old rail lines behind our five trails.

Several railroads served the Monadnock region all of which eventually came under ownership or control by the Boston and Maine. Here is a little history about the ones that came to make up our rail trail system.

CheshireAshuelotPeterborough and HillsboroughMonadnockFort Hill

Cheshire Branch

Historic photo or postcard to come

The Cheshire Railroad was built between 1847 and 1849 and ran between Ashburnham, Massachusetts and Bellows Falls, Vermont. In 1900 it came under control of the Boston and Maine which operated it until the early 1970’s. During it’s later operation, it was mainly a bridge route with only a few on-line customers. Passenger service operated until 1958. One of the most important freight trains on the Cheshire was the milk train which ran daily from Bellow Falls to Boston. Most of the line north and south of Keene was abandoned by the Boston and Maine in 1972, but about three quarters of a mile of the Cheshire is still in service at North Walpole where the Green Mountain Railroad has engine facilities and car storage. The remainder of the Cheshire Branch in Keene was abandoned in 1984.

In 1995, the state of New Hampshire purchased the Cheshire Branch right of way and today, the Cheshire Rail Trail is the longest in the Monadnock region at ~41 miles in length. Over the past few years most of the trail in Keene, south of Keene, and north to Westmoreland have been restored. In Keene, the last section, which will include bridges over route 101 and Swanzey Factory road, is planned to be restored in the next few years. It is also hoped that the trail will be restored in Massachusetts to Winchendon for meet up with the Monadnock Branch and the North Central Pathway.

Ashuelot Branch

Historic photo or postcard to come

The Ashuelot Branch was built between 1849 and 1851 and ran between Northfield, Massachusetts and Keene, New Hampshire. Most of the ~24 mile right of way followed the path of the Ashuelot river where numerous customers were located. These included several paper mills, a wood flour mill, a box factory, and a tannery.

The Ashuelot Branch crossed the Connecticut River once and the Ashuelot River four times. The original Connecticut River bridge was an impressive upside down covered bridge. It was replaced with a metal bridge in 1889. The four identical bridges that are used to cross the Ashuelot River were manufactured by Boston Bridge Works.

After major portions of the Cheshire Branch were abandoned, the Ashuelot Branch was used to reach the yard and customers in Keene. Passenger service on the Ashuelot Brance ended in 1958, but due to the number of on-line customers, freight service continued until late 1983. The last year of operation was performed by the Green Mountain Railroad and two of their box cars still sit stranded on a siding near the location of one of the paper mills in Hinsdale. In 1995, the state of New Hampshire purchased the Ashuelot Branch right of way for what is now the Ashuelot Rail Trail.

Peterborough and Hillsborough Branch

Historic photo or postcard to come

The Peterborough and Hillsboro Branch was built between 1877 and 1878. The line crossed the Manchester and Keene at Elmwood Junction in Hancock. It featured covered bridges in Bennington and Hillsborough as well as a wooden trestle in Hillsborough. In Hillsborough the line joined up with the Contoocook River Railroad that continued on to Henniker and Coontoocook. From Contoocook tracks also went on to Claremont and Concord.

As freight traffic declined, the line north of Bennington and south of Elmwood Junction was abandoned. One of the most important customers remaining on the line was the Monadnock Paper Mill. At Elmwood Junction, Magoon’s curve was built in 1952 to tie in the Manchester and Keene line to eliminate switching from one line to the other and to provide better service to the paper mill.

Following abandonment by the Boston and Maine in 1984, the state of New Hampshire purchased the line from Milford to Bennington in hopes of providing continued rail service to the paper mill but freight service beyond the quarry in Milford never materialized. The tracks on this line remain in place, but haven’t had any maintenance for forty plus years. The right of way north of Bennington and south of Elmwood Junction are now rail trails. At Elmwood a number of historical markers have been placed to indicate where buildings and railroad service facilities were located at this once busy junction.

Monadnock Branch

Historic photo or postcard to come

The Monadnock Branch was built between 1869 and 1871 and ran between Winchendon, Massachusetts and Peterborough, New Hampshire. The line had a number of on-line customers including W W Cross, D D Bean, Noone Mills, and the Peterborough Basket Company as well as passenger service. At Peterborough, it joined up with the Peterborough and Hillsboro, allowing traffic all the way to Concord.

Passenger service ended in 1953. As freight traffic declined, the line north of Jaffrey was abandoned in 1972 and from Jaffrey south in 1984. In 1999, the state of New Hampshire purchased the Monadnock Branch right of way from the Massachusetts state line to Jaffrey for what is now the ~7.5 mile long Monadnock Rail Trail. Planning is underway by the Town of Jaffrey to extend the trail north in the direction of Peterborough. It is also hoped that the trail will be restored in Massachusetts to Winchendon for meet up with the Cheshire Branch and the North Central Pathway.

Fort Hill Branch

Historic photo or postcard to come

The Fort Hill Branch was built between 1911 and 1912 by the Boston and Maine to bypass Central of Vermont trackage between Northfield, Massachusetts and Brattleboro, Vermont. It used the Ashuelot Branch track and Connecticut River bridge between Northfield, Massachusetts and Dole Junction, New Hampshire, then continued to North Hinsdale, New Hampshire where a new bridge was built to re-cross the Connecticut River into Brattleboro.

The line operated until 1970 when one of the piers on the Connecticut River bridge tilted and the Boston and Maine decided not to repair it. After 1970, the line was used to access the Ashuelot Branch and, in turn, the remaining customers in Keene.

The right of way was purchased by the State of New Hampshire in 1994 and is now the ~7 mile long Fort Hill Rail Trail. It connects with the Ashuelot Rail Trail near Dole Junction where they share a trail head. Work is underway in Brattleboro, Vermont to build a pathway from downtown to the Connecticut River bridge. In the near future, it is hoped that the rails will be removed and the bridge will be re-decked to allow for access to the Fort Hill Rail Trail.

Five trails, one connected network

107 miles of rail corridor run through southwest New Hampshire and reach into Vermont and Massachusetts. The map shows how far along each stretch is today.

  • Cheshire45.3 mi
    Bellows Falls, VT to Winchendon, MA
  • Ashuelot21.2 mi
    Keene to Hinsdale
  • Peterborough to Hillsborough20.1 mi
    Monadnock region, north
  • Monadnock15.4 mi
    Peterborough south to Winchendon, plus a 4 mi connector
  • Fort Hill8.1 mi
    Hinsdale to Brattleboro, VT
